Imperial

/im-PEER-ee-uhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is imperial is relating to an empire or its rulers.

Imperial — no source sentence supplied.

Worked Example

The museum's new wing displays silk robes embroidered with dragons that only the emperor was permitted to wear. Beside them sit the jade seals he used to stamp decrees sent to distant provinces under his rule.

Everything in the exhibit belongs to the world of an emperor and the vast territory he governed, which is exactly what imperial describes. It is more precise than 'royal,' because royal fits any king or queen, while imperial ties specifically to an empire and its rulers.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

regal: Regal describes a look or bearing — dignified and splendid, the way a queen carries herself. A stranger's posture can be regal. Imperial is not about manner; it ties a thing to an actual empire and its rulers, like an imperial decree stamped with the emperor's seal.

sovereign: Sovereign means holding supreme, independent power to rule — a sovereign nation answers to no higher authority. Imperial does not name the power itself; it describes whatever belongs to an empire and its rulers. A small island country can be fully sovereign with nothing imperial about it.

majestic: Majestic means grand and awe-inspiring to behold — a majestic mountain or cathedral needs no ruler at all. Imperial grandeur belongs specifically to an empire: a palace is imperial because of the emperor behind it, not merely because it is impressive to look at.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

common: ordinary, without noble rank or grandeur

humble: modest and low in rank

Where it sits · how high and wide the rule reaches — official → noble → royal → imperial

official vs. imperial: Official is far weaker than imperial — an official building simply belongs to a government, while an imperial one belongs to an empire and its ruling family.

noble vs. imperial: Noble is weaker than imperial; a noble family holds a high rank, but an imperial family rules over an entire empire.

royal vs. imperial: Royal is slightly weaker than imperial — royal describes the king or queen of one kingdom, while imperial describes an emperor who rules many lands at once.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — imperi

root — imperi: empire; supreme command (Latin (imperium))

suffix — -al

suffix — -al: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Imperi (empire, supreme command) + -al (relating to): imperial means relating to an empire — or to the emperor who commands it.

Use the root in a new word: emperor

Word Choice

Imperial carries a grand, often historical or ceremonial tone (imperial palace, imperial decree) and fits best describing something tied to an empire's rule or grandeur rather than ordinary present-day political power.
